speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to my office. To help pinpoint the cause of your knee pain after increasing your activity, can you tell me exactly where the pain is located and what makes it worse?

speaker: Patient
text: 23-year-old female. The patient presents with knee pain that started yesterday and has been steadily worsening. She cites recent participation in volleyball involving repetitive pivoting and twisting movements as a possible cause. She was advised at her last physical exam that weight loss could be beneficial for her health.

speaker: Doctor
text: That sounds like a classic presentation for a meniscal or ligamentous injury given the pivoting; does the pain localize to the joint line, and do you feel any locking or instability when you walk? REQUEST TEST: Physical exam for McMurray and Lachman tests.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Physical exam findings indicate tenderness over the medial aspect of the tibia just inferior to the patella. Special tests for ligamentous instability (including Lachman and McMurray equivalents) are negative. No audible clicking, locking, or joint line tenderness elicited during specific provocation tests.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Knee pain, specifically over the medial aspect of the tibia just inferior to the patella. I also have Recent weight loss attempt, Increased physical activity.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), currently managed with oral contraceptive pills. Social history: Has recently joined a volleyball team.

speaker: Patient
text: Denies any fever, recent injuries, swelling or discoloration of the knee, or previous similar complaints. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Pneumonia and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: That is highly unusual given your symptoms of knee pain and recent volleyball activity; pneumonia does not present with localized joint pain. Can you describe exactly where the pain is when you touch it, and does it hurt to bend your knee or squat? REQUEST TEST: Knee_X-Ray.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: X-Ray_Knee: No fracture, dislocation, or appreciable joint effusion.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the clear X-ray results; since there is no fracture or effusion, the pain is likely soft tissue or mechanical in origin. Given the pivoting injury and absence of swelling, do you feel any clicking, catching, or a sensation that the knee "gives way" during movement? REQUEST IMAGES: MRI_Knee_Sagittal

speaker: Patient
text: Denies any fever, recent injuries, swelling or discoloration of the knee, or previous similar complaints. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Pneumonia and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Patellar Tendinitis (Jumper's Knee). The clinical picture of pain worsening with repetitive jumping/pivoting in a young athlete, combined with negative X-rays and absence of meniscal symptoms, points to a soft tissue overuse injury rather than the pneumonia previously suggested.
